title: The Tiny Island People Chose Because It Had No Mosquitoes
question: Why do people live on Santa Cruz del Islote?
message: This video tells curious adults that people crowded onto one of the smallest islands off Colombia's Caribbean coast for a very ordinary reason, rest from the sea and no mosquitoes, and then built the island bigger with their own hands.
angle: People live on Santa Cruz del Islote because fishermen found a mosquito-free rock in the middle of their fishing grounds and built it into a home with coral and stone, and family, fishing and tourism keep them there, despite drinking water that comes by boat, power that depends on a generator and solar panels, and a sea that keeps creeping into the houses.

scenes.narration: The island is called Santa Cruz del Islote, off Colombia's Caribbean coast. Newspapers often call it one of the most densely populated islands in the world, although estimates vary on how many people actually live here. Around it are islands with beaches, palm trees and plenty of room. And yet families crowded onto this one. The reason turned out to be wonderfully ordinary. It has to do with sleep, fish and a very small enemy. I packed a huge backpack, because I like to be prepared. That was my first mistake.

scenes.narration: The boat from Cartagena takes about two hours. I sat at the front and got splashed the whole way. From a distance, the island looks like a pile of houses floating on the sea, as if someone forgot to draw the land. Up close, there is land. Just not much. The island covers about one hectare. That's about two soccer fields. On it are around a hundred houses, mostly one storey, a school, a restaurant and a small square with a cross. The cross gave the island its name. There are no roads and no cars. There is nowhere for a car to go. I looked for a place to put my bag down. I am still looking.

scenes.narration: I decided to walk around the island before lunch. I finished before I was hungry. Then I tried a shortcut between a pair of houses. My backpack tried it too. Only one of us made it through. A kid walked past, looked at me, looked at the backpack, and kept walking with the kind of politeness that hurts. I took the backpack off and carried it in front of me like a sofa. Lesson for this island: bring less. Then bring less again. By lunchtime, the backpack and I were no longer speaking.

scenes.narration: So why here? I had a theory. Treasure. A small island, a long time ago, surely somebody buried something. I asked about treasure. Nobody had any. I checked under a loose stone. Under the stone was more island. I checked under that. Still island. Then I asked about the past, and the story I got was much better. About a hundred and fifty years ago, this was a bare little island with nobody on it. Fishermen working these waters used it to rest and to hide from storms. And then, as locals tell it, they noticed something strange. Night came, and nothing bit them.

scenes.narration: Here is why that matters. The neighbouring islands have mangroves and beaches, the kind of wet, quiet places mosquitoes love. This island had neither. Locals say that is why the mosquitoes stayed away. Picture a party where every guest is invited except the one who always bites. You would stay at that party too. So the fishermen stayed. And because the island was small, they made it bigger. They piled up coral, stone, shells and things the sea brought them, and later cement, and the island grew. Some of the ground I walked on had been built by somebody's great-grandfather.

scenes.narration: I did not take the story on trust. That evening I sat on the edge of the island with one arm stretched out over the water, like bait. On the next island, I could practically hear the mosquitoes planning dinner. Here, nothing. I waited. I waved the arm a little, to be more appetising. Still nothing. At midnight I gave up and went to bed with the spray in my hand, unopened, like a sword I never had to use. In the morning I checked my arm. Not a single bump. I have never been so offended to be ignored.

scenes.narration: Next question. How many people live here? I assumed this would be easy on an island this size. It is not. A figure you see everywhere is about twelve hundred. A man who has lived here his whole life told CNN it was more like nine hundred. Colombia's national census in twenty eighteen counted a little over four hundred. Estimates vary, a lot. Picture a jar of jelly beans at a fair. Everyone guesses, nobody agrees, and the jar keeps changing, because people come and go by boat for work, school and family. I bought a clicker counter anyway. It did not help.

scenes.narration: I stopped counting after a while. Whatever the real number is, the island is full, and everyone seems to know everyone. Doors stand open. Nobody hurries, because nowhere on the island is far enough away to hurry to. Kids run between houses that are almost touching. The walls are painted in bright colours, and a few years ago residents and muralists painted nine murals together across the island. I sat in the little square in the evening, next to the cross, and the whole island seemed to pass by at least once. Somebody's radio was playing. Somebody's dinner smelled better than mine. I realised I had not used my spray once. I changed my mind. Maybe small is not so bad.

scenes.narration: I spent a full day watching how the island runs. Early morning: the boats go out. Fishing is still how most families here make a living. Mid-morning: I went looking for a tap. There is no natural fresh water on an island built from coral. The Colombian Navy has brought drinking water by boat to these islands. A bank even donated a machine that pulls drinking water out of the humid air, which sounds like magic and is actually condensation. Doctors come by boat too. On a health brigade organised with the maritime authority in twenty twenty-three, they saw six hundred and thirteen people here in one visit. Noon: I drank my water very slowly.

scenes.narration: Afternoon: power. In twenty twenty-one Colombia's energy ministry installed a hybrid plant here, solar panels plus a diesel generator, with a battery bank to keep the lights on. Late afternoon: visitors. Tourism matters more and more, and speedboats bring day trippers from the resorts on nearby islands. According to one Argentine newspaper, that means around five hundred visitors a day. Some people from here work at those resorts. Evening: the boats come back with fish. By night, I understood. This is not a place people ended up in by accident. It is a working island, and every part of the day has a boat in it.

scenes.narration: For the people here, that is not a funny story. The Guardian reported that islanders sometimes wake to find water in their homes. These islands sit on average only about two metres above the water. That's about six feet. A local report in twenty fourteen found erosion along roughly forty-five percent of the archipelago's coastline. One nearby island, about one hectare, disappeared completely. Global sea levels are expected to rise by up to thirty centimetres by twenty fifty. Imagine a table standing in a bathtub, and someone keeps the tap running. I sat with my wet backpack and thought about it for a long time. A hammock story is funny once. Living with it every high tide is not a joke at all. I changed my mind back.

scenes.narration: So why not move to the mainland, or to a bigger island? On my last day I followed the boats on a map in my notebook. One line went out to the fishing grounds. One went to a resort island next door, carrying people to work. One went toward the coast, for supplies and schools. Every line came back. Over generations some people have moved to neighbouring islands, and young people leave to study. Plenty of them come back. For many families, this is where the fish are, where the work is, and where every neighbour is family or nearly family. One more thing. There is no room here for a cemetery. People are buried on another island. Even that, they have found a way to carry.

scenes.narration: So here is the answer, all of it. Fishermen needed a place to rest in the middle of their fishing grounds. They found a bare island where, as they tell it, nothing bit them at night. They built it bigger with their own hands, and their families stayed for the fish, the work and each other. Would I move there? Honestly, I would love to. The evenings in that square were some of the best of my year. My backpack would not. My verdict is NOPE, and the problem is entirely me. It suits people who love the sea, close neighbours and early mornings. It does not suit anyone who packs like I do, or who needs a tap. I put the spray back on my shelf. Still sealed. What would you give up to live somewhere with no mosquitoes?

verdict.label: NOPE
verdict.reason: Wob packs too much for an island this small, and fresh water by boat plus a rising sea are real costs; the islanders have strong reasons to stay, Wob does not.

claims.quote: On a coast full of empty islands, would you pick the smallest one? These people did.
claims.statement: Santa Cruz del Islote, one of the smallest islands of the San Bernardo archipelago off Colombia's Caribbean coast, is densely inhabited while many nearby islands have few or no permanent residents.

claims.quote: Newspapers often call it one of the most densely populated islands in the world, although estimates vary on how many people actually live here.
claims.statement: Media reports often describe Santa Cruz del Islote as one of the most densely populated islands in the world; the claim depends on population estimates that vary widely.

claims.quote: The boat from Cartagena takes about two hours.
claims.statement: Santa Cruz del Islote is about a two-hour boat ride from Cartagena, Colombia.

claims.quote: The island covers about one hectare. That's about two soccer fields.
claims.statement: Santa Cruz del Islote covers roughly one hectare, about the size of two soccer fields.

claims.quote: On it are around a hundred houses, mostly one storey, a school, a restaurant and a small square with a cross. The cross gave the island its name. There are no roads and no cars.
claims.statement: Santa Cruz del Islote has around 100 mostly one-storey houses, a school, a restaurant and a small square with a cross that gives the island its name, and no roads or cars.

claims.quote: About a hundred and fifty years ago, this was a bare little island with nobody on it. Fishermen working these waters used it to rest and to hide from storms.
claims.statement: About 150 years ago Santa Cruz del Islote was a small uninhabited island that fishermen from Cartagena and Tolú used to rest and to shelter from storms.

claims.quote: And then, as locals tell it, they noticed something strange. Night came, and nothing bit them.
claims.statement: According to a story told by locals, fishermen who spent the night on Santa Cruz del Islote decided to settle there because it had no mosquitoes.

claims.quote: The neighbouring islands have mangroves and beaches, the kind of wet, quiet places mosquitoes love. This island had neither. Locals say that is why the mosquitoes stayed away.
claims.statement: Unlike neighbouring islands with mangroves and beaches, Santa Cruz del Islote has neither, and locals attribute its lack of mosquitoes to this.

claims.quote: They piled up coral, stone, shells and things the sea brought them, and later cement, and the island grew.
claims.statement: Residents expanded Santa Cruz del Islote using coral, stone, shells and debris from the sea, and later cement.

claims.quote: A figure you see everywhere is about twelve hundred. A man who has lived here his whole life told CNN it was more like nine hundred.
claims.statement: A frequently cited population for Santa Cruz del Islote is about 1,200, while a lifelong resident told CNN it was closer to 900.

claims.quote: Colombia's national census in twenty eighteen counted a little over four hundred.
claims.statement: Colombia's 2018 national census (DANE) counted 432 residents in the population centre of Santa Cruz del Islote.

claims.quote: a few years ago residents and muralists painted nine murals together across the island
claims.statement: On Santa Cruz del Islote, the Pintuco Foundation and the Colombian Navy repainted the house facades, and nine murals were created together with the community.

claims.quote: Fishing is still how most families here make a living.
claims.statement: Fishing remains the main livelihood on Santa Cruz del Islote, although tourism is growing.

claims.quote: There is no natural fresh water on an island built from coral. The Colombian Navy has brought drinking water by boat to these islands.
claims.statement: Santa Cruz del Islote has no natural fresh water source, and the Colombian Navy has delivered drinking water by boat to communities in the San Bernardo archipelago including Santa Cruz del Islote.

claims.quote: A bank even donated a machine that pulls drinking water out of the humid air
claims.statement: Bancolombia donated to Santa Cruz del Islote a machine that produces drinking water from water vapour in the air.

claims.quote: Doctors come by boat too. On a health brigade organised with the maritime authority in twenty twenty-three, they saw six hundred and thirteen people here in one visit.
claims.statement: During a 2023 health brigade supported by Colombia's maritime authority (DIMAR) in the San Bernardo archipelago, 613 people were attended on Santa Cruz del Islote.

claims.quote: In twenty twenty-one Colombia's energy ministry installed a hybrid plant here, solar panels plus a diesel generator, with a battery bank to keep the lights on.
claims.statement: In 2021 Colombia's Ministry of Mines and Energy delivered a hybrid solar-diesel power plant to Santa Cruz del Islote, including a new 125 kVA diesel generator and maintenance of its battery bank.

claims.quote: Tourism matters more and more, and speedboats bring day trippers from the resorts on nearby islands.
claims.statement: Tourism is increasingly important to Santa Cruz del Islote; visitors arrive by speedboat from hotels on nearby islands such as Múcura, where some islanders work.

claims.quote: According to one Argentine newspaper, that means around five hundred visitors a day.
claims.statement: According to the Argentine newspaper La Nación, Santa Cruz del Islote receives around 500 tourists a day.

claims.quote: Some people from here work at those resorts.
claims.statement: Some residents of Santa Cruz del Islote work at hotels and resorts on nearby islands such as Múcura.

claims.quote: The Guardian reported that islanders sometimes wake to find water in their homes. These islands sit on average only about two metres above the water. That's about six feet.
claims.statement: The Guardian reported that residents of the San Bernardo islands sometimes wake to find their homes flooded, and that the archipelago sits on average about 2 metres (6 feet) above the waterline.

claims.quote: A local report in twenty fourteen found erosion along roughly forty-five percent of the archipelago's coastline. One nearby island, about one hectare, disappeared completely.
claims.statement: A 2014 local government report found erosion affecting about 45% of the San Bernardo archipelago's coastlines, and Maravilla Island, about one hectare, had disappeared by 2017.

claims.quote: Global sea levels are expected to rise by up to thirty centimetres by twenty fifty.
claims.statement: Global sea levels are expected to rise by up to about 30 cm by 2050.

claims.quote: Over generations some people have moved to neighbouring islands, and young people leave to study.
claims.statement: Because of Santa Cruz del Islote's small size, some residents have moved to neighbouring islands such as Tintipán or Múcura, and students who continue their education leave the island.

claims.quote: Plenty of them come back.
claims.statement: Many students from Santa Cruz del Islote who leave to continue their education later return to the island.

claims.quote: There is no room here for a cemetery. People are buried on another island.
claims.statement: Santa Cruz del Islote has no space for a cemetery, so the dead are buried elsewhere.
